name: Notes and the keyboard
description: Letter names, sharps and flats, enharmonic spelling, and where each note sits on the keyboard.

name: Intervals
description: Distance between two notes measured as a number plus a quality: M3, m3, P5, A4, d5.

name: The major scale
description: The whole-and-half-step pattern that generates every major key, and its spelling rule of one note per letter.

name: Key signatures
description: The circle of fifths, how many sharps or flats each key carries, and how to name a key from its signature.

name: Scale degrees
description: Numbering notes within a key and naming them: tonic, supertonic, mediant, subdominant, dominant, submediant, leading tone.

name: Minor scales
description: Natural, harmonic and melodic minor, and why the seventh degree gets raised.

name: Modes
description: Dorian through Locrian as rotations of the major scale, and the single note that gives each its colour.

name: Triads
description: Stacking two thirds to build major, minor, diminished and augmented triads.

name: Inversions
description: Which chord tone sits in the bass, and why that changes the sound without changing the chord.

name: Diatonic triads
description: The seven triads a key produces, and the fixed pattern of qualities they follow.

name: Seventh chords
description: Adding a seventh above the root: major, minor, dominant, half-diminished and fully diminished.

name: Roman numerals
description: Naming chords by their scale degree and quality so that harmony transposes to any key.

name: Figured bass
description: The 6, 6/4, 6/5, 4/3 and 4/2 figures that show inversion under a Roman numeral.

name: Harmonic function
description: Chords grouped by the job they do: tonic, predominant, dominant.

name: Tonic function
description: I, vi and iii as places of rest, and what makes a chord sound like home.

name: Predominant function
description: IV and ii as the approach to the dominant.

name: Dominant function
description: V and vii° as tension, and the leading tone that pulls back to the tonic.

name: The dominant seventh
description: V7 and the tritone between its third and seventh, which is what actually demands resolution.

name: Cadences
description: Authentic, half, plagal and deceptive: how a phrase closes, and how strongly.

name: Voice leading
description: Moving each voice as little as possible, resolving tendency tones, and avoiding parallel fifths and octaves.

name: Secondary dominants
description: Borrowing a dominant from another key to tonicise a chord: V7/V, V/vi, vii°7/ii.

name: Modulation
description: Changing key for real: pivot chords, direct modulation, and confirming the new key with a cadence.

name: Extended chords
description: Sixths, ninths, elevenths and thirteenths — the chord vocabulary jazz is written in.

name: Altered dominants
description: Raising or lowering the ninth, eleventh or thirteenth of a dominant to make it lean harder: 7b9, 7#9, 7#11, 7b13.

name: Chord progressions
description: The patterns harmony actually moves in: I-V-vi-IV, the circle of fifths, and why some successions feel inevitable.

name: The ii-V-I
description: The cornerstone of jazz harmony: supertonic seventh to dominant seventh to tonic, and the voice leading that binds them.

name: Modal interchange
description: Borrowing chords from the parallel minor or major — bVI, bVII, iv in a major key.

name: Tritone substitution
description: Replacing a dominant with the one a tritone away, because they share the tritone that wants to resolve.

name: The twelve-bar blues
description: Twelve bars, three chords, all of them dominant sevenths, and the turnaround that sends it round again.

name: Counterpoint
description: Two independent lines heard at once: parallel, similar, contrary and oblique motion, and why parallel fifths destroy independence.

name: Species counterpoint
description: First species against a cantus firmus: consonance on every beat, contrary motion wherever possible, and no parallel perfects.
